title: Storm-stable floating land in the open ocean

concept.text: Storm-stable floating land would provide very large, moored deck areas on which people could live and work in unsheltered coastal or open-ocean water through specified severe storms. The goal is land-like usability within a demonstrated environmental envelope: sufficiently controlled motion, acceleration and deformation, together with structural integrity and reliable station keeping. It does not require a perfectly motionless deck in every conceivable sea state.

Conceptual synthesis: the innovation would combine the platform’s interaction with waves, its structural response and its mooring system so that useful performance persists across a large occupied area. A platform several hundred metres across would provide an intermediate demonstration; kilometre-scale floating land would require further evidence. The advance concerns usable floating area, rather than simply building a larger vessel or proving that a floating structure can survive a storm.

significance.text: The research notes identify airports, offshore bases and new urban land as applications considered for very large floating structures. They attribute to Lamas-Pardo, Iglesias and Carral’s 2015 review a central limitation: open-sea wave heights restrict conventional pontoon-type platforms, while offshore alternatives need more reliable and less costly solutions. These are reported source attributions; the supplied material does not include the article text needed to verify their wording or scope.

Conditional significance: if very large platforms could sustain ordinary habitation and work through specified unsheltered storms, with reliable structures and station keeping, they would make offshore deck area usable for activities that currently depend on comparatively stable ground. If construction and lifetime operating costs were also competitive with suitable coastal reclamation projects, this could open a substantial new practical domain for settlement and industry. Cost competitiveness is an additional condition, not an automatic consequence of reducing motion.

The comparison with powered flight is an interpretive analogy: both would make a previously difficult medium available for a wider range of practical uses. It is not evidence that floating land would have the same historical importance or adoption trajectory. The immediate gain would be usable floating area within validated conditions. Particular buildings, industrial processes, utilities and long-term occupation would require additional qualification, and the breakthrough would neither establish deep-seafloor industry nor resolve the legal status of floating settlements.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is an integrated hydrodynamic, structural and station-keeping arrangement that maintains land-like deck performance over very large areas during specified severe storms in unsheltered water. Relevant engineering challenges include rigid-body motion, local and global accelerations, elastic deformation, structural loads and mooring survival. Hydroelasticity—the interaction between water forces and structural bending—is an important candidate concern, but the supplied evidence does not establish it as the sole or dominant barrier.

Engineering synthesis: a flexible, mat-like platform can respond to waves by bending, while reducing overall motion with a semi-submersible arrangement does not by itself establish suitability for ordinary buildings or fixed industrial equipment. These are useful distinctions between design approaches, rather than verified performance conclusions about particular platforms in the supplied record. Increasing size also does not, by itself, guarantee lower motion: the distribution of deformation, acceleration and loads across the occupied deck must be demonstrated.

Technical performance, scale and affordability are separate hurdles. A successful several-hundred-metre demonstration would not establish kilometre-scale behaviour, long-term durability or economical replication. Widespread deployment would also require convincing construction, maintenance and lifetime operating costs; otherwise a technically successful platform could remain a specialised megaproject.

current_state.text: The research notes describe Japan’s Mega-Float Phase II model as 1,000 m long, 121 m wide and 3 m deep, moored in Tokyo Bay during 1999–2000. They attribute aircraft take-offs and landings, and an aim of measuring hydroelastic response in high waves such as a typhoon, to the abstract of ISOPE-I-02-038, dated 26 May 2002. Those quantitative details and activities are retained as reported historical claims: no saved abstract or full paper was supplied for verification.

As described, Mega-Float was a sheltered-bay airport experiment. Aircraft trials would demonstrate a useful application under the conditions actually encountered, but would not establish storm-stable floating land in unsheltered water. An intention to measure typhoon-related response also does not establish that a specified severe storm occurred, that measurements were completed, or that land-like motion limits were met throughout it. The supplied material does not resolve those distinctions.

The notes identify the U.S. Office of Naval Research’s Mobile Offshore Base programme, approximately 1997–2000, as an investigation of a military platform roughly 1–2 km in scale, including substantial hydrodynamic work. They attribute to Remmers’s 2005 Marine Structures article a mixed conclusion: the programme only partly met its feasibility and cost objective, found no apparent technical obstacle that decisively ruled it out, but left challenges and did not reach a definite overall answer. This describes an incomplete assessment, not a demonstrated operational platform or an established finding of impossibility.

The research identifies abstract-level access for the Remmers article. No copy of that abstract or the full article accompanies the supplied review, so the programme dates, scale and reported conclusions cannot be checked here against their surrounding qualifications. In particular, a reported absence of decisive technical obstacles should not be expanded into proof of overall feasibility, affordability or storm performance.

The notes identify a review by Lamas-Pardo, Iglesias and Carral in Ocean Engineering, volume 109, dated 15 November 2015, with DOI 10.1016/j.oceaneng.2015.09.012. They report that it treats open-sea wave height as a limitation for pontoon-type very large floating structures and calls for lower costs and more reliable offshore solutions. Without the retained article text, the precise applicability of those conclusions to different designs remains unverified; they should not be treated as a universal prohibition on floating land.

The historical precedents therefore motivate the proposed gap—demonstrated storm-stable, land-like use in unsheltered water—but do not establish its present-day status. The supplied record contains no dated recent-search findings establishing whether that gap remained open on 1 November 2026. Missing source copies and recent coverage limit what can be concluded; they do not show that the reported historical results are false or that later demonstrations do not exist.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a platform at least several hundred metres across in unsheltered coastal or open-ocean water during a documented severe storm. Define the environmental conditions in advance, including the relevant wave and weather conditions, exposure duration and occupied deck areas. A sheltered-bay prototype or a paper design would not meet this proposed scope. The size and test conditions are proposed milestones, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Before testing, select applicable existing human-exposure criteria and state the acceleration metrics, frequency weighting, measurement locations and exposure durations used to assess them. Specify separate limits for deck slope and deformation, structural integrity and station keeping. Shipboard criteria for human work could inform the human-motion assessment, but would not automatically qualify buildings, equipment or industrial processes. Any such claimed use needs its own stated requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Before testing, select applicable existing human-exposure criteria and

completion_criteria.text: Measure performance across the claimed occupied areas throughout the specified storm, and document post-storm condition, loss of service and repair needs. Remaining on station and avoiding drydock would be relevant observations, but neither alone would establish acceptable condition: substantial damage or repairs afloat could still have occurred. Evidence should connect the measured motions and loads to continued safe use and the claimed level of functionality.
completion_criteria.label: Measure performance across the claimed occupied areas throughout

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: make the design description, instrumentation, calibration, environmental measurements and analysis methods sufficiently available for independent assessment, and repeat the demonstration across materially different relevant storm conditions. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within an environmental envelope, rather than literal universality. Kilometre-scale behaviour, long-term occupation and durability, and cost competitiveness would each require separate evidence beyond the initial storm demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility requirement

related_concepts.text: Scope comparison with MNE-01, Ship-scale collapse of turbulent skin friction; MNE-02, Merchant ships freed from the displacement-hull speed barrier; MNE-03, Seawater magnetohydrodynamic propulsion at propeller-class efficiency; and MNE-04, Controlled, sustained supercavitating travel: these roster entries concern resistance, speed or propulsion of moving vessels. MNE-09 concerns the usability of large moored areas under wave loading. Progress in vessel movement would not by itself demonstrate floating-land performance, and storm-stable floating land would not establish those transport breakthroughs.

Scope comparison with MNE-05, Basin-scale underwater positioning without surfacing; MNE-06, Through-seawater links beyond the acoustic range–rate ceiling; and MNE-10, Coherent observability of the deep-ocean volume: positioning, communications and observation could potentially support platform monitoring or offshore operations. These are possible supporting relationships inferred from the roster titles. They remain distinct capabilities and do not supply the required structural response, motion performance or station keeping.

Scope comparison with MNE-07, Persistent abyssal work, with depth no longer the cost driver, and MNE-08, Work-class underwater vehicles powered by the ocean: a floating platform could conditionally serve as a surface base for underwater activity. It would not itself solve deep-water access, depth-related costs or underwater vehicle power. Conversely, capable underwater vehicles would not establish habitable, storm-stable surface area.

The research also describes a historical still-deck ship idea, outside the supplied ID roster: a deck remaining still in any sea state without added mass or power. It overlaps MNE-09 where motion control enables floating land, but imposes stronger and different conditions. MNE-09 permits defined environmental limits and does not require zero power or zero added mass. Ordinary stabilization of an underway ship remains a smaller capability and does not acquire a separate ID in this record.

change_log.change: Preserved MNE-09 and its title while defining land-like performance within specified environmental conditions.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent without requiring perfect stillness or universal storm performance.

change_log.change: Replaced the assertion that hydroelasticity is the barrier with an integrated account of deformation, rigid-body motion, accelerations, structural loads and mooring survival.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not establish a single dominant barrier.

change_log.change: Separated the initial technical demonstration, kilometre-scale validation and economic competitiveness.
change_log.reason: Success at one scale or in motion reduction does not establish scalability or affordable deployment.

change_log.change: Retained the reported Mega-Float dimensions, dates and aircraft trials, and the Mobile Offshore Base dates and scale, with explicit attribution and access qualifications.
change_log.reason: Useful quantitative detail should be preserved without presenting uncaptured source content as independently verified.

change_log.change: Distinguished the Mega-Float typhoon-response measurement aim from demonstrated severe-storm performance, and preserved the Mobile Offshore Base assessment’s qualified conclusion.
change_log.reason: Research intentions and incomplete feasibility assessments do not establish operational completion.

change_log.change: Paraphrased the reported 2015 pontoon limitation and bounded its interpretation.
change_log.reason: The exact passage and its scope cannot be verified from the supplied material; it should not become a universal impossibility claim.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed test protocol and replaced absence of drydock repair as a sufficient outcome with documented condition, service loss and repair needs.
change_log.reason: Human-exposure criteria and repair location alone cannot establish structural condition or suitability for particular uses.

change_log.change: Preserved the conditional revolutionary argument and powered-flight analogy while distinguishing direct usable area from downstream applications.
change_log.reason: The analogy is a judgment, and buildings, industry, utilities and long-term occupation require additional validation.

change_log.change: Added explicit reproducibility expectations, finite-test boundaries and comparisons with every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Completion needs assessable evidence, while related capabilities should remain distinct.

unresolved_issues: The three supplied source entries contain no retained documents. Their identity, exact contents and the historical quantitative attributions remain unverified in this record.
It remains unclear whether Mega-Float encountered and measured a relevant severe storm, and what motions, deformation and operational performance were recorded.
The full qualifications surrounding the Mobile Offshore Base feasibility and cost conclusions remain unavailable; abstract-level access was reported but no abstract copy was supplied.
The scope of the 2015 review’s pontoon limitation across designs and environmental conditions remains unresolved.
No recent-search findings establish whether an unsheltered storm-stable floating-land demonstration existed by 1 November 2026.
Applicable human-exposure criteria, storm conditions, deck slope and deformation limits, and requirements for specific buildings or industrial uses have not been selected.
The relative importance of hydroelasticity, rigid-body motion, structural loads and station keeping is unresolved for any particular proposed design.
Kilometre-scale performance, long-term durability and occupation, competitive lifetime costs and legal status require separate evidence or decisions.
